allow.reason: Login, signup, magic-link, OAuth, and clearing session cookies. These run before a session exists.
QStash job callbacks. Authorized by the QStash signature, not a user session.
Scheduled cron handlers. Authorized by the cron secret, not a user session.
Inbound webhooks such as GitHub and Resend. Authorized by the provider signature, not a user session.
Stripe webhook. Authorized by the Stripe signature, not a user session.
Slack Events API webhook. Authorized by Slack's signing secret, not a user session.
Slack slash-command webhook. Authorized by Slack's signing secret, not a user session.
Slack OAuth redirect. The browser returns here with Slack's code, not a session cookie.
Figma OAuth callback. The browser returns here with Figma's code, not a session cookie.
Email unsubscribe. A signed token is the authorization so a logged-out recipient can stop mail.
Public share-link lookup. The share id is the capability; there is no user session.
Browser crash beacon. It only logs, so a signed-out client can report a crash.
Client error intake. Public so the browser can report a failure without a session.
Public demo guest flow. It creates a temporary guest instead of requiring a session.
Build-id probe. Public and contains no account data, so an open tab can detect a deploy.
Legacy tutorial-finished ping. It returns success and stores nothing.
PostHog exception webhook. Authorized by the Svix webhook signature, not a user session.
CLI login finishes here. The one-time code in the body is read and deleted from redis before a token is minted.
MCP token refresh. The bearer token is verified by validateMcpAuth before a new token is issued.
